subChunks.title: Measurement, Units & Data Analysis

storyBeats.txt: In 1999, Theodora said, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one engineering team used imperial units and another used metric. The spacecraft entered Mars's atmosphere at the wrong angle and was destroyed. The cost: $327 million. The cause: a number without its units is not a measurement.

Science is built on measurement — but measurement is not just reading a number from an instrument. It is knowing what you are measuring, in what units, with what precision, and with what confidence. A result without an uncertainty estimate is not complete. A graph without axis labels is not evidence.

Statistics are what allow scientists to distinguish signal from noise — to decide whether the pattern they see is real or merely a coincidence of small sample size. Without statistics, science is guesswork dressed as certainty.

subChunks.hookHtml: Measurement is the foundation of empirical science. But measurement is not simply recording a number — it requires choosing appropriate units, understanding precision and accuracy, quantifying uncertainty, and analysing data to extract meaningful patterns. The tools of measurement and data analysis allow scientists to decide whether their results are real, whether they are consistent with a hypothesis, and how confident they can be in their conclusions.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The SI System

The International System of Units (SI) is the globally agreed standard for scientific measurement. Seven base units:

QuantityUnitSymbol
Lengthmetrem
Masskilogramkg
Timeseconds
Electric currentampereA
TemperaturekelvinK
Amount of substancemolemol
Luminous intensitycandelacd

All other SI units are derived from these seven (e.g., Newton = kg·m·s⁻²; Joule = kg·m²·s⁻²). SI prefixes allow convenient expression of very large or small quantities: pico (10⁻¹²), nano (10⁻⁹), micro (10⁻⁶), milli (10⁻³), centi (10⁻²), kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), tera (10¹²).

Accuracy and Precision

Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true (accepted) value. Affected by systematic errors — consistent offsets from the true value caused by faulty equipment, incorrect calibration, or experimental bias. Systematic errors shift all measurements in the same direction.

Precision: how reproducible a measurement is; how tightly clustered repeated measurements are. Affected by random errors — unpredictable variations in measured values due to limitations of instruments and human judgment. Can be reduced by averaging many measurements.

A measurement can be precise but inaccurate (consistent but wrong — systematic error), or accurate but imprecise (right on average but widely scattered — high random error). The goal is both: accurate and precise.

Types of Experimental Variables

  • Independent variable: The variable deliberately changed by the experimenter.
  • Dependent variable: The variable measured in response to changes in the independent variable.
  • Control variables: All other variables kept constant to ensure any change in the dependent variable is caused by the independent variable.
  • Control experiment: A parallel experiment run identically except the independent variable is held at a reference level — allows comparison to show whether any observed effect is due to the independent variable.

Describing Data: Mean, Median, Mode, Range, Standard Deviation

  • Mean: Sum of values / number of values. Sensitive to outliers.
  • Median: Middle value when data are ordered. Robust to outliers.
  • Mode: Most frequently occurring value.
  • Range: Maximum − minimum.
  • Standard deviation (SD): Average spread of data around the mean. Small SD = tightly clustered data; large SD = widely spread. For a normal distribution: ~68% of data lie within 1 SD of the mean; ~95% within 2 SD.

Correlation and Causation

A correlation is a statistical association between two variables: as one increases, the other tends to increase (positive correlation) or decrease (negative correlation). The correlation coefficient (r) ranges from −1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive); r = 0 indicates no linear relationship.

Correlation ≠ causation. A famous example: ice cream sales are positively correlated with drowning rates. The confounding variable is summer temperature — both ice cream sales and outdoor swimming increase in hot weather. Without controlled experiments, correlation alone cannot establish a causal relationship.

Sample Size and Statistical Significance

Small samples produce unreliable estimates. The larger the sample, the more reliable the mean and the smaller the standard error. Statistical significance (the p-value) tells you the probability of observing results as extreme as those obtained if there were no real effect. A p-value < 0.05 (5%) is the conventional threshold for claiming a result is statistically significant — meaning there is less than 5% probability the result occurred by chance alone. P-values do not tell you the size or practical importance of an effect.

Graphs: Choosing and Interpreting

Graph choice depends on data type:

  • Line graph: Continuous data over time or continuous independent variable — e.g., temperature over 24 hours.
  • Bar chart: Comparison of means across discrete categories — e.g., enzyme activity at different pH values.
  • Scatter graph: Relationship between two continuous variables — look for correlation and fit a line of best fit (trendline).
  • Histogram: Frequency distribution of continuous data — e.g., distribution of heights in a population.

Error bars on graphs represent ±1 SD (spread of data) or ±1 Standard Error of the Mean (confidence in the mean). If error bars for two groups do not overlap, their means are likely significantly different.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why finding a correlation between two things does not prove that one causes the other — using an amusing or counter-intuitive example.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A student measures the height of 5 seedlings (in cm): 12.3, 11.8, 13.1, 12.5, 14.0. (1) Calculate the mean height. (2) Calculate the range. (3) One seedling is an outlier at 14.0 cm. Is the mean or median a better measure of central tendency here, and why? (4) The student's ruler has a zero error of +0.3 cm (all measurements are 0.3 cm too large). What type of error is this, and how does it affect accuracy and precision? (5) If the student wants to determine whether fertiliser increases seedling height, what control experiment should they run?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Mean = (12.3 + 11.8 + 13.1 + 12.5 + 14.0) / 5 = 63.7 / 5 = 12.74 cm.

(2) Range = 14.0 − 11.8 = 2.2 cm.

(3) With only 5 data points and one potential outlier (14.0 cm), the median is more robust. To find the median: order the values: 11.8, 12.3, 12.5, 13.1, 14.0 — the median is the middle value = 12.5 cm. The mean (12.74) is pulled upward by the 14.0 outlier; the median (12.5) is unaffected. However, with such a small sample it is difficult to be certain 14.0 is a true outlier rather than natural variation. The student should investigate why that seedling is taller.

(4) A zero error of +0.3 cm is a systematic error: it consistently shifts all measurements in the same direction (all values 0.3 cm too high). This reduces accuracy (measurements are consistently wrong by 0.3 cm) but does not affect precision (the relative differences between measurements remain correct). The corrected heights are: 12.0, 11.5, 12.8, 12.2, 13.7 cm. Systematic errors cannot be reduced by taking more measurements — the instrument must be calibrated correctly.

(5) Control experiment: grow an identical batch of seedlings under exactly the same conditions (same soil, pot size, light, temperature, watering volume) but without adding fertiliser. Measure heights of both groups (fertilised and control) over the same time period. Any difference in mean height between the groups can then be attributed to the fertiliser (independent variable) rather than other factors — assuming all control variables are identical.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A pharmaceutical company tests a new drug by giving it to 100 patients and measuring their blood pressure reduction after 4 weeks. The mean reduction is 8 mmHg with a standard deviation of 12 mmHg. The p-value comparing this to the control group (who received a placebo) is 0.03. (1) Explain what the p-value of 0.03 means. (2) The standard deviation (12 mmHg) is larger than the mean effect (8 mmHg). What does this tell you about the variation in individual responses? (3) Explain why a statistically significant result does not necessarily mean the drug is clinically useful. (4) The control group received a placebo rather than nothing at all. Why is a placebo-controlled trial important?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) A p-value of 0.03 means: if there were no true effect of the drug (null hypothesis), there would be only a 3% probability of observing a mean reduction as large as 8 mmHg (or larger) by chance in a sample of this size. Since 3% < 5% (the conventional significance threshold), the result is statistically significant — we reject the null hypothesis. It does NOT mean there is a 97% probability the drug works, nor that the drug is clinically important; it only quantifies how surprising the observed result would be if the drug had no effect.

(2) SD = 12 mmHg is 1.5× the mean effect. This indicates very wide variability in individual responses: many patients may experience little or no benefit; some may experience large blood pressure reductions; and some may even see blood pressure increase. The drug's effect varies enormously between individuals. A mean reduction of 8 mmHg with SD 12 means that roughly 68% of patients have reductions between −4 and +20 mmHg — many patients show no benefit or even experience an increase. Population-level statistical significance coexists with large individual-level unpredictability.

(3) Statistical significance depends on sample size — with enough patients, even a trivially small effect (e.g., 0.1 mmHg reduction) could be statistically significant. Clinical significance asks: is the effect large enough to matter to patients? A clinically meaningful blood pressure reduction for treating hypertension is typically ≥5 mmHg; 8 mmHg meets this threshold. But clinical utility also depends on: the side-effect profile; cost and availability; whether patients who benefit can be identified in advance; and how the drug compares to existing treatments. Statistical significance is a necessary but not sufficient condition for clinical usefulness.

(4) Placebo control is essential because of the placebo effect: patients who believe they are receiving treatment often show genuine physiological improvements — reduced blood pressure, reduced pain, improved mood — even when given an inactive substance. If the control group received nothing, any observed improvement in the drug group could be partly or entirely due to the psychological expectation of benefit, not the drug itself. By giving the control group a placebo (identical in appearance to the drug), both groups receive the same psychological expectation; any difference in outcome can then be attributed to the active pharmaceutical ingredient.
learningObjectives: Name the seven SI base units and apply SI prefixes to express measurements in appropriate units.
Distinguish accuracy from precision and systematic errors from random errors, with examples of each.
Calculate mean, standard deviation, and range from a data set and choose an appropriate graph type for a given data set.
Explain why correlation does not imply causation and describe what controls a scientific experiment must include.
commonMistakes: Confusing accuracy and precision — accurate means close to true value; precise means reproducible. A broken clock is accurate twice a day but not precise.
Using mean when data contain outliers or are skewed — median is more appropriate when data are skewed or contain extreme outliers.
Assuming a small p-value means a large or important effect — p-values depend on sample size; even trivial effects can be significant with large enough samples.
Ignoring the need for a control group — without a control, changes in the dependent variable cannot be attributed to the independent variable.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies systematic vs random error in an experimental scenario and explains the appropriate correction.
Accurately calculates mean, median, range, and standard deviation from a small data set.
Explains statistical significance (p-value) correctly without overstating what it means about probability of the hypothesis being true.
Identifies the need for a placebo or other appropriate control in an experimental design.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The probability of obtaining results as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true — conventionally, p < 0.05 is considered statistically significant, though this threshold is arbitrary and increasingly criticised.
SEM = SD / √n — measures uncertainty in the estimated mean (not the spread of individuals); SEM decreases as sample size increases, unlike SD which reflects inherent data variation.

A variable that is related to both the independent and dependent variables and could explain an apparent relationship between them — e.g., age confounds many health studies because older people differ in many ways from younger people.

NASA spacecraft lost in 1999 due to a units mismatch — one team used SI units (newton-seconds); another used imperial (pound-force seconds) in navigation software. Cost: $327 million. Lesson: always check units.
A symmetric, bell-shaped frequency distribution characterised by its mean and standard deviation; approximately 68% of data fall within ±1 SD, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.

questions.questionHtml: A student measures the same mass five times and gets: 102.1, 102.3, 101.9, 102.2, 102.0 g. The true mass is 105.0 g. Which statement best describes these measurements?
options: Accurate and precise — the measurements are consistent and close to true
Precise but not accurate — the measurements are closely clustered around 102.1 g but consistently lower than the true value of 105.0 g
Accurate but not precise — the measurements are randomly scattered around the true value
Neither accurate nor precise — the measurements are both scattered and far from the true value
questions.correctAnswer: Precise but not accurate — the measurements are closely clustered around 102.1 g but consistently lower than the true value of 105.0 g
questions.explanationHtml: Precision: the measurements are tightly clustered (range of 0.4 g, all within 0.3 g of the mean of ~102.1 g) — very precise. Accuracy: the mean (~102.1 g) is consistently ~2.9 g below the true value of 105.0 g — not accurate. This pattern indicates a systematic error (likely a zero offset or calibration error in the balance). The systematic error shifts all measurements equally, preserving precision while destroying accuracy.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds that countries with more cinema screens per capita have higher life expectancy. The correlation coefficient is r = +0.75. Which conclusion is most scientifically appropriate?
options: Cinema attendance causes increased life expectancy through stress reduction
Life expectancy causes more cinemas to be built, because wealthier people live longer
There is a strong positive correlation, but this does not establish causation — both variables are likely related to a confounding variable such as national wealth
The correlation proves that increasing cinema access would improve health outcomes
questions.correctAnswer: There is a strong positive correlation, but this does not establish causation — both variables are likely related to a confounding variable such as national wealth
questions.explanationHtml: r = +0.75 indicates a strong positive correlation, but correlation does not imply causation. Both cinema screens and life expectancy are likely driven by a confounding variable — national wealth (GDP per capita). Wealthier countries can afford more infrastructure (cinemas) and also have better healthcare, nutrition, and sanitation (higher life expectancy). To establish causation, a controlled experiment or detailed causal analysis accounting for confounding variables would be needed — simply observing a correlation is insufficient.

questions.questionHtml: A drug trial reports a p-value of 0.04 with a sample of 10,000 patients, showing a mean reduction in symptom score of 0.2 points on a 100-point scale. A second trial reports p = 0.06 with 50 patients and a mean reduction of 12 points. Which result is more likely to be clinically important, and why does this illustrate a limitation of p-values?
options: The first trial (p = 0.04), because it is statistically significant and statistical significance equals clinical importance

The second trial (p = 0.06), because the 12-point reduction is almost certainly a real and large effect that is statistically insignificant only because of small sample size — illustrating that p-values conflate effect size with sample size
Neither result is meaningful because neither has a p-value below 0.01
The first trial, because larger sample sizes always give more reliable results
questions.correctAnswer: The second trial (p = 0.06), because the 12-point reduction is almost certainly a real and large effect that is statistically insignificant only because of small sample size — illustrating that p-values conflate effect size with sample size
questions.explanationHtml: P-values are sensitive to sample size. The first trial: n=10,000 makes even tiny, clinically trivial effects statistically significant (0.2 points on a 100-point scale is negligible). The second trial: n=50 means even a large real effect (12 points) may not reach p<0.05 — the trial is underpowered. P-values tell you how surprising the result is given the null hypothesis and sample size; they do not directly measure effect size or clinical importance. Good practice requires reporting both effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values. This is a major reason why "statistical significance" alone is an inadequate criterion for scientific or clinical conclusions.
